utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask one of the assistants to go to my office and ask for my case file. I asked that it be brought, but they haven't done it. Perhaps one of the assistants could see my secretary. I don't have my case file. It should have been brought to us here at the bench. Excuse me. First of all, I would like to ask whether the interpreters can hear me. Good afternoon. Good afternoon to the Office of the Prosecutor and to the Defence counsel and to the accused. Then, of course, we wish to welcome our colleague and friend, Judge Almiro Rodrigues. We want to express our gratitude to him, because for the past several days, we know that he has had to replace Judge Riad, and he has a great deal of work. I don't know if I can say the word "titan-like work," that is, the amount of work is titan-like, but that he will be in his full ability and a Judge who will carry out his entire role in the Blaskic trial. I would also like to give you some news from Judge Fouad Riad who is getting better, as best as one can get better after an operation of such magnitude. We will now proceed with our work, but first, there is a little surprise for the Judges. Let me turn to Mr. Hayman. I think Mr. Hayman knows what I'm talking about. We're a bit surprised because we thought that we were going to begin with the testimony of the accused this afternoon. The legal officer of the Trial Chamber, who won't be here for a few days, told me, and I'm sure you must have informed him in a memo that, first of all, we were told that we would be hearing a few other witnesses. We don't want to speak about that at great length, but the dignity of justice, Mr. Hayman, means that when Judges have the feeling, perhaps they are wrong in feeling so, but they do feel that once the three Judges have made a decision, ordinarily, we should respect that decision. That's what we wanted to say. Mr. Hayman, do you wish to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, Judge Rodrigues, only to say I apologise if there was some failure on my part to communicate effectively. What I certainly intended and attempted to tell the Court at the Status Conference of 12 January, 1999 was that, over the remaining ten days of that trial session, we had nine witnesses yet to complete, and that thereafter we expected to call General Blaskic and two other witnesses as to whom there were logistical questions and that I didn't know whether those other witnesses might precede or follow General Blaskic's testimony. Unfortunately, we didn't finish the nine witnesses during those ten or so days. Actually, it was probably seven trial days that we had remaining in that trial session as of the 12th of January. That was our intent. That was accurately, honestly represented to the Court, and I apologise if there was a failure on my part to communicate it as effectively as I should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Of course you're excused, Mr. Hayman. I just simply wanted to say to you that had I been the only one to have made an error in that respect, that is, the idea that for 35 hours scheduled, the accused was going to begin to testify today -- of course, I'm a human being. I'm not a person who is not a person, if you like, who comes from another planet, but that's not the issue here. I asked all of those who were involved in this case -- don't look at the transcript. It's not really indicated in the transcript specifically, that is, by sentence that we're going to start with the accused and then we're going to follow up with the nine witnesses, but throughout our conversations during the last Status Conference, at least the spirit of that conference was that the accused agreed to having Judge Riad be replaced in a very short period because sufficient time was necessary, about a week, and that would take us to about the 8th of February, and then we talked about that, to determine whether we could move the 8th or the 15th. I believe that in any case the spirit, maybe not the letter of the conversation, but it's the spirit, and they were very high level conversations, let us think that the accused needed a specific date, a date had to be set, that he needed time to prepare himself. We spoke about it on several occasions. I don't remember whether we said it would be the 8th or the 15th. We decided on the 15th as the deadline, and I, myself, went to see Ms. McDonald, the President of the Tribunal, to ask her after all types of considerations, briefs, and memos that I wrote in order to justify this Trial Chamber's position in order to make her understand that the accused wanted to begin speaking on his own behalf at a specific time, which I indicated to her. If there was a misunderstanding, Mr. Hayman, of course, we will hear the witnesses, but anything which postpones the trial is prejudicial, both for your client and for the work of justice which we are accomplishing here, but, as you know, both of my colleagues with me are very, very busy with other matters. You'll see that we are now setting up a new schedule, and you'll see that Judge Shahabuddeen, who is the Vice-President of the Tribunal, has a great deal of work in the Appeals Chamber which is busier and busier, and Judge Rodrigues, of course, has a schedule that has to be taken into account as well, and Judge Riad had the same schedule as I did. We have to take this into account in another Trial Chamber in which Judge Rodrigues has participated, but we won't say anything further about that. No need to say any more. Having said what I did say, you can now tell us which witnesses you are going to present to us today. First of all, let me ask you whether they are protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There is no protection for the witness today, Mr. President, and I can tell you and Your Honours that we are on the very eve of the testimony of the accused. We expect him to begin his testimony either tomorrow or Wednesday. So in terms of our earlier discussions and the need for reasonable certainty with respect to the commencement of the testimony of the accused, that is exactly the situation we believed we faced and that we still believe we find ourselves in, and we, again, thank you, Mr. President, and Your Honours and, particularly, you, Judge Rodrigues, for your willingness to join the case so that we can proceed with reasonable certainty and bring the case to conclusion. Today, Mr. President, we will present the testimony of Martin Bell, MP. Mr. Bell is a member of the House of Commons in the United Kingdom. He is a former journalist with the British Broadcasting Corporation and a decorated war correspondent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me be careful here. Mr. Hayman, about how much time do you need for the examination-in-chief because it's that amount of time that the cross-examination is going to depend? About how much time do you need for the examination-in-chief of Mr. Martin Bell?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I estimate one hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. It is now twenty-five after two, so you will be finished at twenty-five after three. Then there will be a break, but we will have a maximum cross-examination of one hour as well. We're going to have the witness, Martin Bell, brought in, please. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing and tell us your name, your first name, your profession, the date and place of your birth, and then you're going to take an oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Martin Bell. I was born in Redisham, England on the 31st of August, 1938. I was, for more than 34 years, a reporter with the BBC. I now sit in the British House of Commons as a member of parliament, an independent member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please remain standing for a few more moments and take an oath which is being given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Martin Bell. You may now be seated. The Tribunal thanks you for having come. We thank you for having come at the request of the Defence in the trial at the International Criminal Tribunal of General Blaskic who, at the time of the facts, was a colonel and who is present in this courtroom at your left. I'm sure you know the legal customs of your own country. These are more or less the same that are here. First, you're going to be asked questions that are asked by the Defence attorney during the examination-in-chief, then the cross-examination, and then any questions that the Judges might want to ask you. Mr. Hayman, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Hayman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, in the nature of introducing yourself further to the Court, tell the Court when your career as a BBC journalist ended and when you began your political career?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: My career as a BBC journalist ended on about the 5th of April, 1997 when, almost accidentally, I was asked to stand as an independent candidate for a constituency in England in rather remarkable circumstances, and I then resigned from the BBC. I won the election and, therefore, am now a member of parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of journalistic work did you do for the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I started off doing all kinds of work, as one does. By the last third of my career, and certainly from 1990 onwards, I did very little but war reporting, first of all, the Gulf War, and then successive wars in Slovenia, Croatia, and finally Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any awards in the course of your journalism career?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I received the OBE, which is a royal award from the hand of the Queen in 1993 and two awards from the professional body, the Royal Television Society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you certain news reports, and we'll pause if the technicians could assist us after each segment so that I can ask you a question or two about those segments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, for your information, these are clips from BBC News footage, video clips. Some of them have a date on the screen of the broadcast, some of them do not. As to the clips that do not have a date, I will be asking the witness if he can help us identify the time frame of the report. The first segment has a date on its screen, the date is the 9th of June, 1993, and if we could play segment number 1, please? If the translation booths could assist us and attempt to provide a translation of the audio track? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, first of all, to the interpreters. I couldn't have the BBC journalist slow down, but I would like to thank you for the work that you've done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, Mr. Bell, who is Justin Webb?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Justin Webb was certainly at that time a staff reporter at the BBC, much as I am. I think he is still working for the BBC, but perhaps wisely he decided to become not a war reporter but a news reader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the report that we have just viewed, was it aired by the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. That looks to me as if it were on our morning or breakfast news programme which relies heavily on two-way interviews of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could now play the second segment of the tape? This segment is dated on the screen. The date is the 16th of August, 1993. If we could play the segment, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a report that you filed with the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next segment does not have a date on the screen. If you could keep in mind while you view it that I will ask you to try and assist us to place it in the proper time frame? If we could now play the third segment, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, Mr. Bell, let me ask you: Is this a report that you filed with the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help the Court and all of us put this report in the proper time frame?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. I think the report itself did that. It was five months after this fighting began. The fighting began in mid April. I returned after a time in Mostar. I returned about mid September, so I guess it would be sometime around late September '93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, the next segment has no date on screen, so if you could watch it with the issue of the proper time frame in mind? Could we play the fourth segment, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a report that you made for the BBC from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help the Court date this report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I remember the day going out on a patrol with the light dragoons. I would put it as, again, late September, early October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could play segment 5, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, is this a report that you filed with the BBC from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you provide a time frame for when that report was made?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think it was a little bit later. The weather had started to turn. I would place it in October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could we now play segment 6, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a news report that you filed from Vitez with the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report appears to reference the coming winter. Can you tell us what season it was in what year?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was autumn 1993. I should think probably October.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could play segment 7, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this also a report that you filed from Vitez with the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it certainly is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what time frame did you file that report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I filed it in the same time frame. We are talking about the autumn of '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could play segment 8, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, who is Humphrey Hawksley?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Humphrey Hawksley is a BBC reporter. At that time, he was based, I believe, in Hong Kong, and he was substituting for me over that Christmas of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the report then was made around Christmastime '93-'94?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could play segment 9? There are 15 segments, Mr. President. We're about two-thirds of the way through. Segment 9, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are the one that makes that decision. You choose what you are going to show. But let me remind you that you have to be finished by twenty-five after three. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a report you filed with the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you date the report for us, at least approximately?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was either very late December 1993 or early January 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reference to a mass grave, can you tell us approximately where that mass grave was located?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The mass grave was on the main road to Poculica, exactly where the frontline had been at one time. It was in no man's land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Poculica being on the road from Vitez to Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: On the road north, the back road to Zenica, yes, the old road to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If segment 10 could be played, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a report that you filed from Vitez with the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village referenced that contained the Dutch transport battalion base, what village was that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That was the village of Santici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you date this report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It would be about the first week of January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could play segment 11, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a report which you filed with the BBC from Opara, Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During what period or season did you file it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: We are talking about the middle of winter. This would still be January 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court in what region Opara was located and why it was a significant access point for Central Bosnia and aid coming in to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: This was south of the Croat enclave in the Lasva Valley, it was the main supply route being used by the British north from Split into the valley, and really at that time the only one they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could play segment 12, please. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a report that you filed with the BBC from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you provide a time frame for that report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: This is also at the time of the battle of Santici at the beginning of January 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It didn't appear very well on this version of the film, but with reference to the eight chained, executed soldiers, whose soldiers were they; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Those were soldiers of the HVO. There was a dawn attack by the Bosnian -- a pre-dawn attack by the Bosnian army in the fog which took the village and got across the road, and these soldiers were surprised in what they must have felt was a safe house. All we know is that when they were found, they were bound and shot. So whether they were shot and then trussed up or held as prisoners and then the house was retaken, something like that would have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If segment 13 could be played, please. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The on-screen date of that broadcast is 11 January, 1994. Is that a report you made with the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a reference in the report to the main road east of Vitez. Which road is that? Could you provide greater specificity?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It's the main road through the valley which leads to Busovaca and Kiseljak. It was the main supply road for the United Nations and, of course, the main road for the Croats as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If segment 14 could be played, please. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The on-screen date of that segment was 12 January, 1994, the day after segment 13. Is that a report that you filed with the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reference to the road in the segment, is that a reference to the same road you described a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the last segment, segment 15, could be played, please. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The on-screen date in segment 15 is the 14th of January, 1994, for the record. Did you file that report from Vitez with the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could the tape be assigned an exhibit number, Mr. President, and I would ask that it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you want to have marking by sequence, by excerpt, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The segments are plainly marked 1 through 15, so I think one number can be assigned to the tape, and then we can distinguish among the segments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be D532/1-15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the 27th of April, 1993. Did you attend a press conference on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can date this in time, the 27th of April was approximately 11 days after the massacre in the village of Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the accused present at this press conference?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it was held in the town hall in Busovaca. Mr. Blaskic was present and so was Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was present?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic, Mr. Kordic, and a lot of journalists, mostly local. This became a regular event in order that the local commanders, military and civilian, could communicate in some way with the population, not to reassure them how well things were going but, as far as I could see, to warn them how grave their situation was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did then Colonel Blaskic address the subject of the massacre in Ahmici at this press conference?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I made some notes at the time which I, with the agreement of the Court, will read. He said he was horrified. He was going to do something about it, that "...a commission is being set up to investigate the atrocities. Whoever did it did it in an organised, systematic way. It was an organised group of people operating to a plan and, therefore, controlled by someone. The culprits must be identified and brought to justice," and Colonel Blaskic said he was appalled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that statement you've just read, is it a quote or near-verbatim quote of what Colonel Blaskic said to the press and to the public at this press conference on the 27th of April, 1993 in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, have you read, in fact, from contemporaneous notes that you made at the time in order to provide the Court with the details of Colonel Blaskic's statements at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of my black notebooks which I always carry with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for being so concise, Mr. Hayman, and going straight to the point of what you wanted to show. I'm now turning towards the Prosecutor's office. Mr. Martin Bell, you're going to be asked by the Prosecutor. By you, Mr. Harmon, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, and welcome, Judge Rodrigues. Good afternoon, Counsel. Welcome, Mr. Bell. Yes, Mr. President, I will be asking questions of Mr. Bell. Will we be taking a break at 3.15, because it would perhaps be better to take a break now and continue, uninterrupted, my questions, rather than ask him questions for five minutes and then interrupt. I leave it to the Court's discretion. I'm prepared to proceed either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, we may as well have the break now. We are supposed to have two breaks. It's going to be a long afternoon. So this might be an opportune time to have a fifteen-minute break, and we shall resume in 15 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay We can begin with the cross-examination now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bell. Welcome to the Tribunal. Let me reintroduce myself, I'm Mark Harmon, and let me reintroduce my colleague to you, Mr. Andrew Cayley. Again, welcome, sir. Let me ask you, Mr. Bell, I have looked with interest at the 15 video clips that were presented here in evidence today, and I know that you produced more than 15 video clips from Bosnia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I must have produced hundreds over three and a half years, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Central Bosnia, approximately how many video clips did you produce?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I would guess roughly 40 or 50 over those nine months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In going through these 15 clips, I noted that approximately seven of these clips occurred in January of 1994, which was approximately seven months after the events at Ahmici; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I noticed that six of the clips were from September or October of 1993, which was about five or six months after the events at Ahmici; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, one of the clips, clip 15, had a picture of the accused, it was dated -- segment 15, and the date on the clip was the 14th of January, and in that clip, you are quoted as something to the effect that Colonel Blaskic had returned to the pocket after a ten-day absence. Do you remember the portion of that clip that I just quoted?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me where Colonel Blaskic had been in those ten days?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Oh, I wasn't following him about because I was in the Lasva Valley and he was not, but there was a time -- the siege lasted really until the agreement in February '94. The only way he could get out -- and there was a time, I suppose, from about September '93, the HVO ran in, at huge risk, helicopters which did sort of a corkscrew landing, and they got some of their seriously wounded out through there, but very occasionally, once or twice Colonel Blaskic would leave for the HVO headquarters and then come back again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he went?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I'm assuming -- I mean, if a field commander leaves, he's normally going to his headquarters, but I never asked him about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me then ask you, Mr. Bell, in respect of his particular absence, did you make inquiry as to anybody in the HVO as to where Colonel Blaskic had been in those ten days, specifically make inquiry, and to whom did you make inquiry and what was the response that you received?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I would sometimes ask his liaison officer at the hotel if he was available, and sometimes he would say he wasn't available and sometimes he would say he's away, but we normally got the information through the British Battalion at Vitez. They would have a pretty good idea of when he was away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me focus your attention on a different subject, Mr. Bell, and that is the press conferences. You have quoted from a statement made by Colonel Blaskic at one press conference, but did you attend more than one press conference?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I have notes of having attended two, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware, are you not, and you have informed the Office of the Prosecutor, that those press conferences, either through information that you received through your colleagues, were held once a week in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were public events. I think they were mostly for the benefit of the local press, but they were happy to have us there, and it was helpful to me to know what their thinking was, so I was happy to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher, please, with this next exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 572.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, let me just orient you through this Prosecutor's Exhibit. It is an exhibit that has four pieces to it, and they will be placed on the ELMO which is next to you so that they can be displayed on the monitor, and this is the first photograph -- and if you could come back a little bit on this -- this is a photograph at a conference, a press conference, held with Mr. Blaskic. Do you recognise Mr. Blaskic in that photograph, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To his right, do you recognise the man seated to his right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It's not very good quality, but I assume that that's Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the individual to Mr. Kordic's right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I rather think that that is Mr. Ante Valenta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Valenta?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the man to Mr. Valenta's right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I see him. I couldn't put a name to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name Kostroman, Ignac Kostroman?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, that's not a name known to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you another picture of a press conference, the next photograph in order, and ask you if you can identify at least two of the people in that photograph because you've said you couldn't recognise Mr. Kostroman on the far left of that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It looks, although it's not a very good quality photograph, it looks again like Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me show you the next item in that particular series of documents, and this is even a poorer reproduction, Mr. Bell. I apologise. It may be helpful to you if you pick it up off of the ELMO and inspect it a little closer, but this is a press conference of the regional HVO headquarters after the signing of the maps in New York, and it is in April of 1993. Do you recognise Mr. Blaskic in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It's very hard to tell, but I'd say it's probably him, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Second to the right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Looks like it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To Mr. Blaskic's right, who do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, the picture quality is getting worse and worse --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: -- I assume it's Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To Mr. Kordic's right, do you recognise the individual?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It's too blurred for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, again, let me just lastly turn to the last of the series in this particular series of photographs and poorly reproduced photographs. Do you recognise the individual to the far right in that particular press conference?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I'd say that's Colonel Blaskic again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the middle, who do you recognise, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure. It's too vague for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If I told you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the witness is looking at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And he says that the picture is too blurred. I wonder if he would do better if he looked at the ELMO itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your suggestion, Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you take a look at the copied reproduction?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I would assume it's Mr. Kordic. I wouldn't absolutely swear by it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This also is an image taken from a press conference of the regional HVO headquarters in Central Bosnia. Now, let me ask you, sir, when you attended the press conference that you've described on the 27th of April, 1993, did the location of where the people were sitting and how they were addressing the audience appear to you to be similar to those that I have shown in these four photographs found in Prosecutor's 572?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I can only actually remember Mr. Valenta from the press conference held on the 12th of May, '93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he hold a -- let's focus on that press conference separately from the press conference where you had this statement that you have noted from Mr. Blaskic. The press conference on the 12th of May, who was present at that particular press conference?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Certainly Colonel Blaskic, certainly Mr. Kordic, certainly Mr. Valenta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they seated in a configuration similar to that which is depicted in the various images found on Prosecutor's 572?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. They sat at one end of the -- it is the old Communist system. They would sit at one end, and the press would sit around the other three sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know the title of Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I knew it. It was some kind of political something, but to be quite honest, after nearly six years, you would have to pressure my memory of what he called himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I informed you that he entitled himself as the HVO deputy president and the deputy president of Herceg-Bosna, is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. There was no doubt that the distinction was made to us that the military account of things was being given by Colonel Blaskic as the military commander, and then Mr. Kordic dealt with other matters on the civilian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Anto Valenta was the deputy president of the HZ-HB government?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I was, because he was announced as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the two press conferences that you attended personally, Mr. Blaskic was present with the political leadership at the same table; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember Valenta at the first of the press conferences. He was certainly at the second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in respect of this particular press conference that you attended on the 27th of April, 1993, you gave us a quotation in which Colonel Blaskic said something to the effect, and I'm going to quote, "I'm horrified. I'm going to do something about it. I'm appalled." He claimed that a commission was going to be set up to investigate Ahmici, and he said, "Whoever did it did it in an organised, systematic way. It was an organised group of people operating to a plan. The culprits must be identified and brought to justice." Now, you were present at that particular press conference, Mr. Bell, and other representatives of the foreign press were also present at that press conference; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put that particular statement in the context, if I can, because -- let me focus you back a little bit to April 16th, 1993 because prior to the HVO attacks in Ahmici on the 16th of April, the world's attention was pretty much focused on the events that were taking place in Srebrenica; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was not there on the 16th of April. You might be prejudging when you call them "HVO attacks."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me ask you this,

utterances.speaker: MR. BELL
utterances.text: Wasn't the world's attention focused on Srebrenica on the 16th of April? That was the thrust of my question.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have the first film clip? There's two film clips I'd like to show the Court and I'd like to show Mr. Bell. If I could have the first of those two film clips rolled at this time, and if I could have the lights dimmed? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have, with the assistance of the usher, this is a transcript, Mr. President, for Your Honours and for counsel, of the first clip that I have just shown and the second clip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while that's being handed out, Mr. Bell, let me ask you: The statement that you have attributed to Mr. Blaskic on the 27th of April occurred after the HVO seized for themselves what they believed was theirs under the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I believe that it was clear to us at the time that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was having the effect of, if you like, adding fuel to the fire. I also do remember that, in the military briefings that I was given on my arrival four days after the Ahmici massacre at a time when nobody knew the Ahmici massacre had taken place, the British briefing was that ethnic cleansing was spreading like wildfire through the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, my question was, however, Mr. Bell, the statement that was made by Mr. Blaskic was made after this particular news broadcast was made by you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was made after the massacre at Ahmici became known, surely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the statement that was made by Mr. Blaskic, Colonel Blaskic, was made after that particular news broadcast that we have just seen was aired internationally?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That particular one, you have the date of it. I don't know when it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That particular one was on the 20th of April -- I'm sorry, on the 20th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I doubt if I was in a position to broadcast on the 20th of April. I think I arrived there on the 20th of April without any means of transmission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I can clarify that, and I will be glad to clarify that with the Court, that's my understanding of when that clip was made, and I will come back to you, Mr. Bell, momentarily with a clarification on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if I could have the second clip shown. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, was that a report you filed with the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What day was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was broadcast on the 23rd. At the time, our satellite dish was still in Tuzla, so we actually would have shot it the day before. We were out at that time doing same-day transmissions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the film footage we see was taken on the 22nd of April, and it was transmitted the 23rd, the next day?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you say that every house, every Muslim house, that was in Ahmici had been burned down?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Burned down or ruined in one way or another, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the effect of your significant report that was aired on the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think it had a global effect. You never know what effect -- I mean, I was not broadcasting to have an effect. I was broadcasting to tell the truth. But I do believe it had a tremendous effect in the outside world, not least because it showed people that this was not a simple war of Muslims against Serbs. There were other dimensions people were only beginning to understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was one of the effects, Mr. Bell, that it brought attention to a new conflict, a new, unknown conflict that was now occurring and erupting in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It had been on the verge of happening, I think, since about January, with growing tension between Muslims and Croats as a result of the sudden influx into that territory of Muslims and Croats who had been driven out by the Serbs of Prijedor especially, which upset the very delicate ethnic balance in Central Bosnia. Sooner or later, there was a spark that ignited that explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I have read a portion of a newspaper article from the Daily Mail that's dated the 24th of April, and it indicates that your reporting, Mr. Bell, "... dramatically switched the attention away from the Srebrenica atrocities in Srebrenica which dominated the news a week ago." Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the last clip that we saw, we saw Ambassador Thebault from the ECMM, and Ambassador Thebault made reports about what he had seen in the village of Ahmici, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the reports that you filed as a BBC news broadcaster, BRITBAT filed its own reports to its chain of command, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Both of its chain of commands. It had two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you agree with me that the effect of those numerous reports, Ambassador Thebault's, yours, BRITBAT's report, brought a lot of pressure to bear on the HVO in Central Bosnia to account for this horrible massacre that had taken place in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's why I believe that Colonel Blaskic made the statement he did at that press conference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the comments of your news reporting as well create other pressures, such as bring pressure to bear on the Republic of Croatia, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that directly, but I did hear later that they were embarrassed by it. For instance, Margaret Thatcher cancelled a visit to Zagreb where she was to have received an honorary degree from the university.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I could have Prosecutor's 532 shown to Mr. Bell. I'd like to show you a document, Mr. Bell. Mr. Bell, let me show this to you and orient you through this document. This is a document that is dated, in the upper right-hand corner, the 29th of April, 1993, and it is a meeting of the HZ-HB. It includes the presidency of HZ-HB, the government of HZ-HB HVO, members of the presidency and government of the RBH, presidents of the HVO municipalities, and presidents of the municipalities of HDZ. Approximately --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down a little bit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately 60 people attended this gathering, and Mate Boban presided over this particular meeting. My first question to you, Mr. Bell, is do you know who Mate Boban is and what role he played in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, I know he was a powerful figure in Herceg-Bosna, but we never actually saw him in the valley, as you'd understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, but you reported in Bosnia and you reported extensively on the events involving the HVO. Do you know who he is and what his role was?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: If I did, I'd have to say I've forgotten. He could have been the defence minister down there, but I couldn't be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know it's been a long time, Mr. Bell. I certainly appreciate that sometimes memories do fade, but Mr. Boban was the president of the HZ-HB and he was the commander in chief of Mr. Blaskic. For your information, there's been other evidence presented in this courtroom about Mr. Boban. But let me just direct your attention to page 3 of this particular document, and there's a section on page 3 that deals -- about two-thirds of the way down, it says, "Mr. Ivica Santic, Vitez." Do you know who Mr. Ivica Santic from Vitez was?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No. He was not somebody that I remember having met.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was the mayor of Vitez, and he was one of the attendees, and he is quoted in here, and I will only read a portion of his quotation: "Also pointed out the mistakes of HVO units. No one can justify the crime in Ahmici. Great damage has been done. The reaction of UNPROFOR is devastating for us." Then I'd like to direct your attention lastly, Mr. Bell, to the last page of this document, the remarks of Mr. Boban himself, and he's found toward the bottom of the page, and I will read this to you, Mr. Bell. It says: "Mr. Mate Boban," and it's underscored, "instead of closing remarks, emphasised 1) Individuals on all levels must complete their tasks or leave; 2) In making a decision, certain limiting factors must be taken into account, especially when it concerns the Republic of Croatia. Due to the events in Vitez (the village of Ahmici), EU ministers have almost announced sanctions against Croatia." Returning to my question, Mr. Bell, not only was pressure brought to bear on the authorities of Herceg-Bosna, but would it be fair to say that pressure was also brought to bear on Croatia itself, and that was a matter of concern for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I could well understand that, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when Colonel Blaskic made the remark that you have quoted for us here today, you said Dario Kordic was present with him; isn't that correct? In fact, he was seated alongside of Colonel Blaskic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dario Kordic agree with that remark as well?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I haven't got a record in my notebook of what Dario Kordic said, and at nearly six years away, I couldn't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he disagree with what Colonel Blaskic had said?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was not aware of any disagreement. They were dealing with different things, military and civil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. At any of the two press conferences that you attended, Mr. Bell, where Colonel Blaskic spoke and then Mr. Kordic spoke, did you see Colonel Blaskic ever disagree or take issue with anything that was said by Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Not that I can remember. I do remember at the second news conference a statement by Mr. Valenta, which was so clearly out of line, we felt he was expressing his own private opinions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a statement that was made at the public news conference?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was a statement made at the public news conference, and he handed us a piece of paper, which I still have -- wish I had but I don't, giving the philosophical justification for ethnic cleansing. I mean, I'll read it out to you, if you like. I've got it here. It's in one of these. At the time, we felt it was very out of line because we weren't hearing anything like this from the rest of the leadership. Mr. Valenta said -- was suggesting -- he said, "The movement of populations should be encouraged because people should not be forced to live in places where they feel endangered and insecure." He also gave a great speech about how offensive they found the sounds of the Muezzin, which he compared to church bells which chimed only once a week. This was very, sort of, off-the-wall stuff, and our feeling was that he was speaking for himself, rather than for the community as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic, at that news conference, take issue with the remarks made by Mr. Valenta?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No. His job was to give us an account of the military facts on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kordic take issue with the remarks that were made by Mr. Valenta?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I cannot remember him taking issue with them or he certainly didn't endorse them because I would have remembered it if he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at these conferences, at these press conferences that you attended, some of what was being said, Mr. Bell, was being said for the benefit of the foreign press; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: This is possibly so. The primary purpose of these press conferences was to inform his own people. I mean, I think they started happening before -- we found out about them rather by accident and were admitted, they were not held in order to bend our ears, but I'm sure our presence affected some of the things that were said at them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you reported the events at Ahmici truthfully, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any doubt in your mind that what you reported was accurate reporting to the world about the events at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I'm pretty confidant to this day that I got the events right. I've been reporting war zones long enough to be very careful about atrocity stories, and I only report what I'm sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/58, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Would you tell me exactly which document it is that you're looking for?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me orient you to Prosecution Exhibit 456/48.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a report, a top secret, strictly confidential report, that was issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 24th of April, 1993, and it was issued to the vice-president of the HZ-HB, that person being Dario Kordic, the head of the HZ-HB defence department, and the HVO main headquarter's chief. Please read that to yourself before I ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you have a copy for the Judges, even if it's in English, and then you can ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you allow me a moment, Mr. President, I'll look. I may have another copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you put it on the screen? I'm going to give it to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have provided you with one of the copies from our exhibit set.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you then, Mr. Bell, you have had a chance to read this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, I have now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I say, this is a defence top secret, strictly confidential report of a meeting -- of the events that occurred at a meeting between Colonel Stewart of BRITBAT and Colonel Blaskic, and the subject of that particular meeting was "the massacre of Muslim people in the village of Ahmici in the Vitez municipality and the visit of the Security Council delegation today, 24 April, 1993," and you'll see in that particular document that Colonel Blaskic recounts what Bob Stewart informed him. Toward the bottom of that page, you will see what Colonel Blaskic remarks following the sentence that says "I think that Mr. Boban" who is, I mentioned to you, the president of Herceg-Bosna and Colonel Blaskic's commander in chief, "should have been in Vitez today." The first thing he says is to indicate that the reporting is extremely biased, and I would like to direct your attention to the next page, the third bullet point: "To talk about the extremely one-sided emphasis on suffering of only one people, expressing the suspicion that journalists are being paid to report events untruthfully." Now, I'd like your reaction to that, please, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I don't think the reporting was one-sided. I was certainly never, never paid. A lot of my reporting over that war I have been accused of concentrating too much on the suffering of one side or another. But I would have expected some such response as that. This happened. It happened where it happened. The victims were Muslims. And I'm not surprised to read what I've just read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, Mr. Bell: Are you aware of any commissions ever being set up to investigate Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, sir, I am not. It was certainly promised. I, of course, left Central Bosnia shortly thereafter, I think on the 12th of May, and I was away for quite a long time because Mostar blew up, and I was not aware what had happened subsequently because I didn't return to the valley for some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you your views having reported extensively about the Ahmici massacre. This Court has heard evidence that a conversation took place between Colonel Blaskic and General Duncan.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, no. He would be Colonel Duncan, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then Colonel Duncan, now General Duncan, during which time a question was asked of Colonel Blaskic as to who perpetrated Ahmici, and this conversation took place on or about the 9th of May, 1993. To that question, Colonel Blaskic answered the following, and I would like your reaction to each of these three parts: He indicated that, first of all, this was perpetrated -- the massacre at Ahmici was perpetrated by Serb extremists. What's your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think it's a long way from any Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, he said that the Muslims who had infiltrated the pocket were responsible for the massacre at Ahmici, and what is your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was quite a common tactic among all three peoples of Bosnia, when one of those peoples, whether under orders or not, had done something they shouldn't have done, to blame the victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think the Muslims perpetrated the massacre at Ahmici, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the third comment that Mr. Blaskic gave was that Muslims dressed in HVO uniforms committed the massacre at Ahmici. What is your reaction to that, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not believe that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 380, please. Mr. Bell, let me direct your attention to the second full paragraph, the bottom part of this page, and will you read that to yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, this is an article found in a magazine known as Danas, it was published in October of 1993, some considerable period of time after the events in Ahmici. In this portion that you have just read, you have read the question put by Mr. Lovrenovic, that is: "You investigated a crime in Ahmici. What is the result of the investigation so far?" To which Colonel Blaskic answered: "The investigation is still in progress; information is being gathered. In any case, this is a well-planned scenario in which Muslim forces wanted once again to cast a blemish on units of the HVO before the world community. After the crimes that Muslim forces committed in the areas around the Croatian villages of Lasva, Dusina, Gusti Grab, and other villages in Busovaca Municipality, the case of Ahmici was staged and skilfully shown to foreign reporters and to the EC observer mission, with the assistance of the commander of a British battalion at the time, Bob Stewart. So far, we are certain that the crime was committed by members of the HOS (Croatian Defence Force) in Zenica, which was mostly Muslim, and parts of the Muslim forces of the MOS (Muslim Defence Force), and I have already said that the investigation is continuing. It is certain that the HVO does not stand behind the crime that others desire to attribute to us." I won't read the rest. Now, could I have your reaction to Colonel Blaskic's remarks that were made in October of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think it would be strange if this were done by Muslim units of any kind. It always seemed to me that in the chaos that prevailed at the time, where this was -- what? -- three miles from a British UN base, and they took five days to find it. I always felt that it was done by an out-of-control -- could have been done by an out-of-control element of some kind, and I assume it would have been an out-of-control Croatian element.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This event, as you know, Mr. Bell, took place about four kilometres from Colonel Blaskic's headquarters; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what is your reaction, sir, to the attribution that the perpetrators of this offence were mostly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I just told you, sir. I think it's most unlikely, and I've always thought it was most unlikely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that Ahmici was "a well-planned scenario in which Muslim forces wanted to cast a blemish on units of the HVO"?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think it was a well-planned scenario by somebody who wanted to kill the inhabitants, the Muslim inhabitants, of that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have been a war reporter for a considerable period of time, Mr. Bell. The results of what you saw when you went to Ahmici with Colonel Stewart and Ambassador Thebault was one that showed systematic destruction of a then fairly large Muslim community, a fairly large Muslim village; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is true, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe, Mr. Bell, that the case of Ahmici was skilfully shown to foreign reporters and the EC observer mission with any intent whatsoever to discredit the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think we kind of blundered upon it. As you saw in that report, Colonel Stewart went out with quite a large patrol that morning to try and establish that the cease-fire was working and that the two sides had withdrawn, and when he was up on the high ground, he was told of the massacre in Ahmici and then went down. I had a pretty good sense, after so many years in the business, of when things are being staged, and I didn't -- I'm pretty sure it wasn't staged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, most of the footage that we saw from the 15 clips that you testified about earlier were clips that were, as I said earlier, anywhere from six to nine months or so after the events at Ahmici; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Those ones, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, at that point in time, the Muslims were conducting a counter-offensive down onto the pocket, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. More than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bell, thank you very much. I appreciate it. I have concluded my examination, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Re-examination by Mr. Hayman now, please. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Hayman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, you've been asked about these two press conferences you attended. Tell the Court, please, what was the format of the press conferences? Was it a discussion or were separate statements given by the individuals on the podium?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I felt that this was very much in the mode that prevailed in the old Titoist days. There would be long speeches by both the main principal figures: First, Colonel Blaskic, and then Mr. Kordic, which could go on for twenty minutes or even half an hour at a time, and then there would be time for questions. I mean, the whole thing would always last at least an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What types of topics would Colonel Blaskic address at these press conferences that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Almost always he would paint a dark picture of what was happening around him of how they were willing to fight to every man if they had to, of the extent to which they were outnumbered by six to one, seven to one, even ten to one. He would produce the casualty figures that far, the dead and wounded, and generally indicate that the Croats were in a pretty dire position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he restrict himself to military matters?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he covered -- yes, he covered the military side of things. Of course, it became political when he would -- when he would claim that the United Nations was biased against the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about intolerant or racist statements by figures such as Anto Valenta. At any of these press conferences or, indeed, ever in your contacts with Colonel Blaskic, did you ever hear him express intolerant, racist, or ethnically discriminatory views towards persons of Muslim origin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, sir, I never did. I always regarded him as a correct military man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the seriousness of the Croat military position that you learned about at these briefings you attended, did you yourself agree that indeed the military plight of the Croats in the Lasva Valley for which Colonel Blaskic had responsibility, was indeed as serious as he was depicting at these press conferences?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, we thought it quite possible that the pocket could fall. In that one attack in April 1994, its central communication road was cut, with the Muslims on either side of it. I believe their predicament was desperate throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were shown some minutes of apparently a meeting that happened outside of the Lasva Valley on the 29th of April, 1993. That was Exhibit, for the record -- 532, for the record. Was the press conference you attended at which you heard Colonel Blaskic condemn the atrocities in Ahmici, was that two days earlier, on the 27th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you've already said that that press conference on the 27th of April was principally attended by local representatives of the press and the media; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That's correct. There may have been one news agency representative, but otherwise, it was just ourselves with the international media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that forum the best forum available to Colonel Blaskic to reach the population, civilians and military, in the Lasva Valley, to use as a vehicle for condemning the killings of innocent civilians and atrocities committed in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think it was the only forum he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he used it, didn't he --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: He used it, he used it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- to condemn the attack in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he condemned the attack in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were shown two taped segments: The first one we were told was from the 20th of April, but were you in a position to broadcast a show -- excuse me, a report on the 20th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, sir. I keep records of what I did and when I did it, and on the 20th, I was in a position only to use the satellite telephone from the army's press house in Vitez. I was desperately calling for reinforcements, I needed a transmission system, and I wasn't able to broadcast the first pictures of the situation in Vitez until the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the reporter, the news reader, I think -- is that what you call them in your business?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the person that sits at the desk at the main facility and figures out a catchy lead-in with which to introduce your piece; that's a news reader?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: In England it is, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe the news reader on that story says something to this effect: "Croats are consolidating their position by driving out Muslims because of the Vance-Owen Plan," or somehow in relation to the Vance-Owen Plan; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you saw on the ground in Central Bosnia in April and May of 1993, was there a plan to ethnically cleanse Muslims from the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I believe there was a separation of peoples because of the danger. We had fairly close relationships with the UN at that time, not the usual antagonism that occurs between the press and the military, and we exchanged information. I mean, I knew things they didn't know, and they knew things I didn't know, and we were not certainly told at the time of any plan for a premeditated attack by either side; rather, my notes, when I read them back now, tell me that they saw it as ethnic cleansing catching like wildfire from village to village. That was the -- "wildfire" was the term they used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you describe the situation on the ground in April of 1993? Can you sum it up for this Court?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe it was chaotic. The two peoples who shared the valley each felt suddenly threatened by the other. Who shot first, I don't know. It was a time of great fear and panic on both sides. Civil wars are always the worst wars, and I think it was worse because they knew each other and had been neighbours. But utter chaos, utter chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could Prosecutor's Exhibit 29 be retrieved and placed on the ELMO, please? I can ask a few questions while that's being retrieved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second clip you were shown, including the very disturbing scenes and report that you did film in Ahmici on the 22nd of April, you've said that was broadcast on the 23rd of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the actual film was made on the 22nd of April; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Correct. It was carried by courier on the morning of the 23rd, carried by courier to Sarajevo as an edited report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it was broadcast that night on the news?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was first broadcast at 1.00 in the afternoon and again at 6.00 and again at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was broadcast in the United States as well, I believe, on ABC News?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in contact with the British battalion on the prior day, the 21st of April?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Colonel Stewart and the British battalion, how did they come to find the magnitude, the true magnitude of the atrocities and the killing of civilians that occurred in Ahmici on the 22nd of April? How did they come to find it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: On the 21st, they had been putting out reconnaissance missions to the villages round about to see how bad things were. I accompanied some of these reconnaissance units, and it was then that we came across the fallen minaret which you saw in that report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: But we didn't know then what had happened further up in the village, and it was only on the next day, the 22nd, when we went round the top on the high ground, because Colonel Stewart wanted to see if the separation of forces was working under the cease-fire agreement, that's -- we then came down into Ahmici from the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that after some local BH army fighters told Colonel Stewart what was down there and that he should go down there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Exactly, sir. You saw it on my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I misspoke, Mr. President. The Exhibit I wanted was 29C, not 29, but with the Court's permission, I'll hand my version of 29C, and this can be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So counting back, Mr. Bell, from the 22nd of April, when the British battalion discovered the nature and expanse or extent of the atrocity in Ahmici, counting back to the day it occurred, the 16th of April, we have how many days? Count with me. Twenty-one, 20, 19, 18, 17, 16. We have six days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 16th and during those ensuing six days -- if we could zoom in slightly on the Exhibit 29C, please? This is a map of the Vitez and its environs, with, I believe, rings that indicate one kilometre each. If we could zoom in a bit more, please? Thank you. Perhaps looking at the original and not at the video screen, can you find Ahmici? I believe it's one of the orange villages to the right, upper right, perhaps, the far right of the orange illuminated villages?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Sorry. My eyes are not really good enough for this because the name of the village has been wiped over with the orange. That's the problem. It could be this one (indicating).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: One of the villages which is orange on the right on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For the record, I can help the witness, Mr. President. I believe it's the upper of the two far right here --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think it's this one (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You need to point on the --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Sorry. I think it's this one (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. I think the witness has identified it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where was the British base? Can you find that on this Exhibit 29C?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: This, sir, and the British base was way over -- it should be over here somewhere (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see Stara Bila and Mosunj going up the road towards Travnik or Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me help the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think it's around here somewhere (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stara Bila.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you indicate that one more time, please?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Over here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think you've gone a little too far. You see the hill with Stara Bila?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Ring number 4 on the road from Vitez towards Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
