utterances.text: If you would count with me on the roads by the rings then, going from that location to Ahmici, we have one, two --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Three, four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- three, four, five, six, seven. About eight kilometres; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during those six days, as well as on the 16th, the British battalion, they had a fleet of armed personnel carriers or tanks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Not tanks, armoured personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With a gun?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO have such transportation? Did you see Colonel Blaskic in April of 1993 inspecting troops with the aid of his own armoured personnel carriers?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did it take six days for the British battalion, with all their equipment and their armoured transport and their intelligence units, to discover the extent of the atrocities in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Partly because of the degree of chaos prevailing at the time but partly because of their mandate. Under their mandate, they would have been absolutely entitled just to have sat in their camp and stayed safe, but they were brave people and they tried to help, and they hoped, simply by driving around with their armoured vehicles, they were clearing some of the bodies away, trying to reassure people, trying to set up cease-fires, but it was pretty chaotic, and the commanders, of course, were responsible for the lives of their men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was a dangerous time to be out?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was one of the most dangerous times of the whole war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about different units in Vitez and statements Colonel Blaskic made about HVO and differentiating among different units. I'd like to ask you about one of those units you referred to in your cross-examination. Darko Kraljevic, how would you characterise him?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. It was not a question that I asked. I did not ask that, I did not go into that line of inquiry, and if it's going to be asked, I'd ask that I be permitted to examine this witness further on that subject. But I did not ask any questions on my cross-examination about Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It went far outside the scope of direct. I held my tongue for the sake of time, but he asked about the overall picture, Colonel Blaskic's overall responsibilities, he talked about different units, and I think I should be allowed to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, to clarify the record, I asked Mr. Bell about events to put the statement in context. I did not ask Mr. Bell about units of the HVO; I asked him about the context of that particular statement. So this is, I believe, Mr. President, an inappropriate area in which to conduct a redirect examination. I would ask, if Mr. Hayman goes into this area, that I be permitted to ask Mr. Bell questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You know what I think about the limits, which is always a bit ambiguous in respect of the re-examination and the cross-examination. Ask your question in such a way that it doesn't go too far outside the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll ask only one question on this subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about the accused and HVO units and statements the accused made characterising different HVO units. Could you characterise Darko Kraljevic in terms of his role in the war in Vitez, briefly?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: He was an extraordinary character, and I had the impression that although he held a very vulnerable part of the frontline with men under his command, I felt he was not really under Colonel Blaskic's command. He had his own -- he was kind of a warlord, he was very charismatic, a brave man, if you like. He operated out of something called the Cafe Kapan, and I didn't think he was -- there was not what you might call a normal chain of command operating there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, but if that testimony sounds unfamiliar, it is because I didn't ask anything about it, and therefore, I would ask that I be permitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you also asked questions, Mr. Harmon, about Anto Valenta, Mate Boban, on politics, on Kordic, you asked questions on cross-examination. Let a little bit of fluidity be here so that the Judges can have a general idea about the matter. Have you finished your question about Darko Kraljevic, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am finished. I have a couple more questions and I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, let's not start a whole debate about Darko Kraljevic. You know, the Judges have been working since the 23rd of June, 1997. They too are beginning to be familiar with Darko Kraljevic. All right. If you don't mind, move to another question, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked whether you agreed or disagreed with other statements attributed to Colonel Blaskic concerning events in Ahmici attributed to him, according to the Prosecutor, by Alastair Duncan or other statements set forth in plaintiff's -- Prosecutor's Exhibit, excuse me, 380. One thing the Prosecutor didn't tell you in that series of questions is that on or about the 10th of May, 1993, Colonel Blaskic ordered an investigation internally within the HVO of events in Ahmici. Did he ever share that with you or with the public?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, he just made the announcement on the 27th of April, but you have to remember that about the 12th of May, I think, after his press conference, I left there, so I was not in touch with him for quite some weeks or months after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit 380 speaks of unbalanced reporting. Do you know whether the international media covered any of the events in January 1993, including the massacres at Dusina and Lasva? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I don't recall that. They certainly covered the massacre at Uzdol in December 1993 in which Croats were murdered by Muslims. I mean, we were aware of many massacres, and we got access to some. We didn't get access to others, but there was no predetermination, "Yes, we will report this kind of atrocity but not that kind of atrocity." It's not the way we work or the way we should have worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you for coming, Mr. Bell. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. Judge Shahabuddeen, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, may I begin by congratulating you. As a war correspondent, you were the given the OBE, and I can see why. In several of the clips we saw, you must have been pretty close to the line of fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. You were operating as a professional, dispassionate reporter?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, there was a conflict, an armed conflict, between two sides. Would I be correct --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- in interpreting you this way, that you recognise that losses and atrocities were suffered by each side?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There was no monopoly of wrongdoing in that war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: There wasn't any. Yes. Now, would I also be correct in understanding you to be recognising that the pendulum was apt to swing with time? At one time, the advantage would lay with one side; at another time, it would lie with the other?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, through you, the Defence introduced 15 television clips. Would I be correct in supposing that those clips related to events between, I think, August 1993 and February 1994 when the pendulum had swung over to the Muslim side? They were on the offensive.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that the plight -- the position of the Croats was fairly difficult throughout the whole period from April to the following February, in that they were under siege for that entire time, and, indeed, their main supply route was cut towards the end of that time. So I would not have thought that the pendulum swung significantly in their favour in the course of those nine months. What they were able to do was to get themselves a more professional defence force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Now, where would you say the pendulum was during the period April/May 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think that the situation was very adverse for the Croats at that time. They then managed to stabilise it only for other parts of that area to break into open warfare, notably, Gornji Vakuf and Bugojna, which were further south.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Was there some part of the evidence introduced through you in which there was a reference to the Muslim forces having moved from being a ragtag body into a more disciplined and organised entity?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think, sir, that applied to both the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So would the case be this, that the idea of the pendulum swinging from one side to another was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, it was correct in other parts of the war, in that the war only ended when the pendulum started swinging against the Serbs, when the Croats started seizing large parts of land, and we're talking here of late '94/'95. The situation in the Lasva Valley was somewhat different, except that I think that it was absolutely desperate for the Croats in April '93, and, to some extent, they had that stabilised by mid summer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, during the period covered by these 15 television clips, were you shown in any of these clips with the BiH forces?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was with the BiH forces from time to time. It was not, as far as I can remember, included in those clips. We were based in a Croat-held town, and so that part of the war was filmed mostly from their side of the lines, but we did get around to the other side at other times, certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: During the period covered by these 15 television clips, did the Muslim side suffer any losses or atrocities?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they certainly did. The Ahmici massacre was one. That was, of course, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That's before this period.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: We're talking about April '93 to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No, no, I was talking about the period covered by the 15 clips.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Did the Muslim side suffer casualties? They certainly did. Whether atrocities, I'm not sure. I only talk of atrocities that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So you did not report any atrocities that might have been suffered by the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was not aware of having been shown any more, though that mass grave which was the subject of one of those reports, I'm not clear to this day of the identity of the victims found in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. Now, you spoke of gas. You're an experienced war correspondent. Did you see any of the kind of damage or injury which you would expect could be produced by the use of gas?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: If there was gas used in that war, it was nothing more than teargas. We're not talking about the kind of gas -- that is, we're not talking about nerve gas or anthrax or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I appreciate that clarification. I was a little puzzled myself.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was a low-tech war, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Blaskic made a statement, in the course of which he condemned the happenings at Ahmici. Now, as a trained war correspondent, was it your view that a military commander, faced with the events at Ahmici, had any alternative but to condemn what happened?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I'm sure, sir, that as a human being, he had no alternative but to condemn what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would it have been your view that a separate and distinct question was the attribution of responsibility for what happened at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think there is no doubt that what happened was within his area of responsibility on the map, but I don't know more than that. I mean, I can only testify to the chaos that prevailed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, as to the attribution of responsibility, the learned Prosecutor adverted to certain positions suggested by Colonel Blaskic. One, he said, "Well, the Serbs might have done it." Two, he said, "The Muslims might have done it." Three, he said, "Some Muslims might have dressed up in HVO uniforms and done it." You didn't accept any of those three possibilities as serious?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, tell the Court this, Mr. Bell: You knew Colonel Blaskic, and you had a reaction within you --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Do you wish to know what that reaction was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What would have been your reaction if you were told that these were the three possibilities suggested by Colonel Blaskic? Would you say that he seriously believed in those three possibilities or that he was presenting them tactically?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I suppose he was presenting them tactically. I think he found it hard to know what to say under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I come to Mr. Ante Valenta. You had some difficulties placing him, but I believe in the end, you tugged at your memory and recollected that he held an important position.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. He held an important position on paper. I got the impression he was not a man with much practical power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Was it your impression that he had any input into the formation and establishment of political goals and objectives?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I can't give a good answer to that question, Your Honour. I do remember thinking that I hoped he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you said your personal -- you didn't say "personal." I'm saying "personal." You said that your evaluation of the statement which he made was this, that it represented his personal views and not the collective position of the podium.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Not the collective position of that podium. I don't doubt there were many people in Herzegovina who held those views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You described Colonel Blaskic as a correct military officer?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I always found him to be so, and he dealt very straight with me from the start to the end. He was one of the more approachable of the commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say that a correct military officer is an officer who, although he does not meddle with political matters, stands ready to execute the will of the political directorate, whatever that will is?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I would qualify that, that when a civil war suddenly erupts in a chaotic situation there with, I think, inadequate communications, I think he would be hard put to find out what the collective political will was for a number of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, you have been the most engaging witness, and I conclude by repeating my congratulations to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. Judge Rodrigues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, along with my colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen, I would like to congratulate you for the work that you've done and also for the information that you have brought to the Tribunal. I have got two questions to ask you. From some of the information that you provided here, you said that Ahmici was a kind of pressure that was put on the HVO and drew the attention of the International Community to the events in that area; however, my colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen, asked whether the press conference that the accused gave was a strategic one, and you said that there was a certain way of coordinating things within the field of strategy. I'm asking you this question because I believe that you were a very good observer and an independent one in respect of the events, and so that's why I'm asking you this. In the area of tactics, could one find any kind of cooperation between the HVO and other forces, including the HV, or was that not the case?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was certainly the case that in the fighting between Muslims and Croats later in the summer, there was substantial HV help, especially to the Croat forces in Gornji Vakuf. There would be army vehicles with their license plates taken off, which always meant to us that that was HV, and they started to get heavy weapons as well. As for the time we're speaking of in the first days of the fighting in the Lasva Valley, I think the HVO and other units were left pretty well to fend for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, one might set up the following relations: On one side is the strategy, which is matched by coordination and action, and on the other side, there are tactics which, in the field, are expressed by cooperation. Could this kind of relationship be set up?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think that Colonel Blaskic was left to devise his own tactics, though I'm sure that as the weeks and months passed, he did not want for advice from Herzegovina, but initially, I think he was having to make it up as he went along, and I'm sure the same applied on the BiH side as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The other question that I would like to ask is related to the first. As an independent observer, you lived through these events very close up. You were very close to where things were happening. This has to do with the statement that you made about General Blaskic's press conference, who was a colonel at that time, did you feel, because you said that you had experienced the war more on the Croatian side than on the other one, was there any kind of official policy or unofficial policy in which there was only -- or was it kind of a cohesive policy? Did things change according to circumstances so that you would conclude that there was an official and an unofficial policy? What would your opinion be about that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I mean, we spent the most time on the Croat side more or less by accident. Over the war as a whole, I would say that I spent more time on the BiH side. I suppose we came to -- what happens, Your Honour, is that you come to sympathise with soldiers as individuals, whichever army they're fighting for, because they don't want to be there. They want the war to end. I think, in a way, in the course of this war, we humanised our war reporting a little bit. If you're asking if there was a political agenda, there was not a political agenda, except in this sense, that we were on the side of peace, and we wanted the United Nations to succeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bell. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. We are almost finished now, Mr. Bell. I have one or two questions I'd like to ask you. I didn't quite understand when you referred to the expression "a correct officer." You are a member of a great nation with a great army. What is a correct military person?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: This was something that I borrowed actually from the Serbs. Because I was not, they thought -- they didn't think I was in their favour, but they didn't think that I was biased against them, and they called me correct, and I borrowed this notion of correctness, which is someone just doing the job which they are paid to do and not overstepping any bounds. It was a phrase I borrowed from the old JNA, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, the commander of a military operative zone in a conflict, since he is correct, should only be involved with military issues, according to that definition?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, though I have to say that obviously the United Nations, although soldiers, were definitely taking part in political activities because, to a large extent, they were the International Community on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So here's my question: You saw the accused in the press conference. You saw him with politicians, with Ante Valenta, with Kordic, which you yourself referred to as political people, politicians. Would you say that the presence of the commander of the operative zone would mean that he shared the political ideas of the commanders in that area?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I would very much doubt if he shared Mr. Valenta's ideas. I believe he was fairly close to Mr. Kordic, but their jobs were different. I mean, if I could point out to you that on the bombing of Iraq by the British and Americans last December, the press conferences were given then in London by the British defence secretary and the chief of the defence staff. This happens. This is a quite common practice. It doesn't mean that the chief of defence staff has to share all the political aspirations of the defence secretary, but for a politician and a soldier to be side by side at a press conference is not unusual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but you are now in politics. You're in parliament. Could you say that in this type of a war, high military responsibility would be given to somebody that did not share the military objectives?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: In this particular conflict, we are speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [indiscernible translation] objectives.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I understand what you mean, Mr. President. In this particular conflict, which was pretty desperate on both sides, I think that whatever Colonel Blaskic felt of the political opinions of the man beside him, he was the man they felt best qualified to fight this war. This was a people at war on both sides. I have no idea to this day what his political opinions are because I never discussed politics with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't speaking about his political opinions today. I'm speaking about the fact that he was part of a political plan. Let me change my question. Would you say that Mr. Kordic or the political leaders had a political purpose in this conflict, and, if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think their political purpose initially was survival as an entity. If they'd been defeated, the Croats would have disappeared from the Lasva Valley forever. They were concerned with survival, as, indeed, in the other sense, were the Muslims. That's the way it was with civil wars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But in the beginning, perhaps you would agree with me when I say that the Lasva Valley belonged to an entity which politically was very well-determined, that is, Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning, of course, it had a very mixed population as well. They lived among each other. I mean, that mosque in Ahmici was about 100 metres from the main road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a final question. In other testimony, apparently, there was a significant presence of the Muslim brigade. Could you say anything about that Muslim brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Is this a question about the Mujahedeen, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: One of the difficulties that we had in approaching the war in the Lasva Valley from both sides was that the Mujahedeen were extremely hostile towards the press and, indeed, towards foreigners, and there was a case in January 1994 when they killed a British aid worker and tried to kill two others. They were certainly a force in inspiring a great deal of fear among the Croats, and they were, I know from my contacts on the BiH side, extremely difficult for the regular Bosnian army forces to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But as a war correspondent, you, yourself, said that you spent more time with the Muslims than you did with the Croats. Did you see them? Did you meet them? Did you question them? Did you have any press conferences? Could you tell us anything concrete about that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The Muslim brigade or the Mujahedeen did not hold press conferences or certainly not for the foreign press. They were extremely hostile to the foreign press. Our contacts with the Bosnian army were through their co-headquarters in Travnik and Zenica and, of course, in Sarajevo. When I tell you I spent most time on the Muslim side of the lines, meaning the Bosnian government side of the lines, I'm referring especially to a long time in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to join my colleagues in not only thanking you but also in congratulating you. You're a man who has shown a great deal of courage throughout this period, and I also thank you for the quality of your testimony in which you always try to take the high ground vis-à-vis this dreadful conflict. All right. We are now completed. You can go back to your work in the House of Commons, and we are going to finish at 6.00. I don't have to -- perhaps we could take a 15-minute break now. I see that the registrar -- did I make a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, no, no, you didn't make a mistake. I wanted to know what we are going to do with D532 and the Prosecutor's evidence 532 and 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would move for admission of the photographs, the set of four photographs, with Colonel Blaskic and others at press conferences, and I would also move for admission of the transcript that is associated with the film clips, and I would move for admission of the film clips themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We're going to take a 15-minute break, and we will resume for about a half hour and work until 6.00. Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I need to inform the Court that we do not have another witness for this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't want there to be misunderstandings. How many witnesses do you have left? You said that the accused would begin to testify on Wednesday. This is Monday. How much time do you have left, up to the point when the accused begins to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have three short witnesses left. I expect them all to conclude tomorrow. Whether the accused will start his testimony tomorrow afternoon or Wednesday at the beginning of the session, I cannot say. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It will probably be on Wednesday, that is, Wednesday afternoon; is that right, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Wednesday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We can say that there are three witnesses left, and they will not take too much time. Mr. Harmon, do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. I would request that these witnesses be identified. We received notice of some witnesses, some three new witnesses, at a late hour, five or six days ago. If these are the three witnesses who Mr. Hayman has identified to us, then, Mr. President, we have not had the notice that is required under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are they protected? Are they protected? Mr. Hayman, they aren't?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Then you can disclose their identity to the Prosecutor. How come that wasn't done yet? Was it Thomas Masic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He's complaining, Mr. President, that he doesn't know the order that they're testifying. They've been disclosed to him. He wants the order. The Court has never ordered us to give an order, although we have always endeavoured to give the order that we believed witnesses would testify in to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Hayman has a way of attributing certain views of mine that he wants to put in the most negative fashion. Let me be perfectly clearly, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we received notice of three witnesses, and we received that notification of three new witnesses, and by our calculation, the seven days' notice runs out on Wednesday, not on Tuesday. So my only question to Mr. Hayman was, are these witnesses who have been disclosed within the framework of the decision or are these the three witnesses that were disclosed at approximately 10.00 or 11.00 at night five days ago?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Judge's microphone, please. The Judge's microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [no translation] ... we cannot continue to argue over questions like that; otherwise, I'm going to settle the issue. Are we talking about your memorandum of 10 February, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I can settle this, Mr. President. One of the witnesses for tomorrow was disclosed on the 5th of January of this year. One of the witnesses who will testify tomorrow was disclosed on the 7th of January of this year. I hope there's no problem with respect to those two witnesses. The third witness who will testify tomorrow was faxed to the Prosecutor on the evening of the 9th of February. That is seven calendar days from tomorrow. If the Prosecutor has not had time to prepare for that witness, we will keep that witness here. He can have overnight to prepare cross, and we'll keep him here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. This time the Presiding Judge is going to settle the issue. Who are the three witnesses we're going to have tomorrow? I don't remember what happened on the 9th of February or the 7th of January, but I want to know which three witnesses we're going to have here tomorrow because now I think that it is time that the accused testify. Is it Ozmanic, Plavcic -- who are the ones who are going to testify tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Anto Plavcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Anto Plavcic. Would you note that down, Mr. Harmon, so that we don't have to repeat this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's one of the January ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Nikica Lovric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I must have it here. All right. As regards everything else, you can come to an agreement if you have any questions. All right. The Tribunal doesn't want to hear about this anymore. What time are we starting tomorrow? At 10.00, is it? All right. The Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.20 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of February, 1999 at 10.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
